A term used to describe any thermodynamic process that occurs with neither a gain nor loss of energy between the system and its surroundings; or any thermodynamic process that occurs without heat entering or leaving a system. Since no heat enters nor leaves the system, heat (Q) is zero, hence the first law of thermodynamic becomes: ΔE in = -W, where ΔE in is the internal energy of the system and W is the work done. This process generally involves a fall or rise in temperature of the system. The term can be applied in several contexts as follows: (i) Electronically adiabatic is a reaction in which there is no change of electronic state or multiplicity. (ii) Vibrational adiabaticity is a reaction in which there is no change of vibrational state during the course of reaction. The term also applies to a process in which excess vibrational energy in the reactants appears as vibrational energy in the products or in which ground-state vibration in the reactants leads to ground state vibration in the products. (iii) Rotational adiabatic is a reaction in which excess rotational energy in the reactants appears as rotational energy in the products or in which ground- state rotation in the reactants leads to ground-state rotation in the products. 2. In the Rice-Ramsperger-Kassel-Marcus (RRKM) theory of unimolecular reactions, a degree of freedom whose quantum number is more or less preserved during energisation.

In geometry and trigonometry, the side of a right-angled triangle that lies between the reference angle (not the right angle) and the right angle. 1. A safety device fitted in motor vehicles consisting of an inflatable plastic bag mounted under the dashboard or on the back of the front seat and also sometimes in the roof and doors. Since the person's momentum must be reduced to zero in a very short time, it implies that the force on the person's body must be very high (Newton's second law of Motion: F = Δ mv /Δ t ). The air bag extends the interval of time over which the person's momentum is reduced to zero and as a result reduces the rate of change of momentum and hence, the force. 2. The properties and laws of sets, which includes the set-theoretic operations of union ( ∪ ), intersection ( ∩ ) and complementation and the relations of set equality and set inclusion. It also provides systematic procedures for evaluating expressions and performing calculations, involving these operations and relations. The binary operations of set union ( ∪ ) and intersection ( ∩ ) satisfy many identities. Several of these identities or laws have the following names: (i) Commutative laws: A ∪ B = B ∪ A and A ∩ B = B ∩ A; (ii) Associative laws: A ∪ (B ∪ C) = (A ∪ B) U C and (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C). (iii) Distributive laws : A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C) and A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C). There are also some more important laws of set algebra. For example, Proposition 3 states that for any subsets A and B of a universal set ∪ , the following identities hold: idempotent laws given by (i) A ∪ A = A and (ii) A ∩ A = A. The de Morgan's laws are given by (i) (A ∪ B)' = A' ∩ B' and (ii) (A ∩ B)' = A' ∪ B' .

An equation of the form f ( x ) = 0, where f is a polynomial. It shows the equality of two expressions formulated by applying to a set of variables, the algebraic operations namely, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, raising to power and extraction of root. An example is 4 x 3 + 6 x 2 - 7 x + 4 = 0.

An expression containing a collection of numbers, variables and signs, positive or negative and arithmetic operations that must make mathematical and logical sense, for example, 5 x 3 - 3 y 2 + 2 xy . Two types exist: simple and compound. Simple algebraic expression has one term, called a monomial, for example, 3 a . Compound algebraic expression has two or more terms: the one with two terms, for example, 4 x + 3 y is a binomial; the one with three terms, for example, 2 x 2 - 3 x + 1, 3 m^-2 n + 5 z , is a trinomial; and the one with more than three terms is a multinomial. Alternatively, an algebraic expression may not contain any individual quantifiers and is expressed only in terms of variables and intended to be interpreted as being true for all members of some set; for example, x ( y + z ) = xy + xz .

An extension field of a base field with the property that every element of the extension is algebraic over the base. Let L/K be an extension of fields. L/K is said to be an algebraic extension field if every element of L is algebraic over K. If L/K is not algebraic and contains transcendental elements then it is a transcendental extension field. An algebraic extension of the rationals is an algebraic number field. For example, the field extension R/Q, that is the field of real numbers as an extension of the field of rational numbers, is transcendental, while the field extensions C/R and Q(√2)/Q are algebraic, where C is the field of complex numbers.

A function that may be expressed in a finite number of terms, of only the elementary algebraic operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and root extraction, for example, f ( x ) = nx 3 + x 4 - 2 x . They are distinguished from transcendental functions, such as the exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions, which can be expressed only by an infinite series. Another way of saying this is that the function f ( x ) is algebraic if y = f ( x ) is a solution of an equation of the form p n ( x ) y n + ... + p 1 ( x ) + p 0 ( x ) = 0, where p 0 ( x ), p 1 ( x ), ..., p n ( x ) are polynomials in x . All polynomials are algebraic. A function that satisfies no such equation is transcendental. There are various types of algebraic functions. A rational function does not have any fractional powers of the variable or variables. Integral functions do not include the operation of division in any of their terms. A homogeneous function is one in which the terms are all of the same degree, i.e., the sum of the indices of the variables in each term is the same for every term. For example, u 4 + u 3 v + u 2 v 2 + uv 3 + v 4 is a rational, integral, homogeneous function of the fourth degree in u and v .

The study of geometries that come from algebra, in particular, from rings. In classical algebraic geometry, the algebra is the ring of polynomials and the geometry is the set of zeros of polynomials, called an algebraic variety . For instance, the unit circle is the set of zeros of x 2 + y 2 = 1 is an algebraic variety, as in all the conic sections.

Let f 1 , ..., f n be polynomials in F[ x 1 ,..., x n ]; { f 1 , ..., f n } are algebraically independent if and only if there is no non-zero polynomial A ∈ F[ y 1 , ..., y n ] such that A( f 1 , ..., f n ) = 0. If the polynomials do not satisfy this, they are said to be algebraically dependent and A is their annihilating polynomial. For example, { x 1 , x 2 } are algebraically independent, but { x 1 , x 2 , x 1 3 + x 2 2 } are not.

The root of a polynomial with integer coefficients, where the coefficient of the highest power is 1. The polynomial is of the form x n + a 1 x n^-1 + ... + a n = 0, where a 1 , ..., a n are integers; For example, x 1 = 2 + 3 is an algebraic integer, since A x 1 2 + 4 x 1 + 1 = 0 . The set of all algebraic integers is closed under addition and multiplication and therefore, a subring of complex numbers denoted by A.

A number that is the root of an algebraic polynomial. For example, in the expression x 2 = 2, the square root of 2 (√2) is an algebraic number because it is a solution of the equation x 2 = 2. Another source defines it as any number that is the root of a polynomial equation with coefficients drawn from a given field, in particular the rationals; in that case, √2 is an algebraic number, but π is not. A number which is not algebraic is called transcendental. The algebraic numbers form a field.

Compounds that contain cumulate double bonds, >C=C=C<, in which three carbon atoms are linked by two adjacent double bonds. The outer carbon atoms are each linked to two other atoms or groups by single bonds. The simplest example is 1,2-propadiene, CH2 =C=CH2 . Allenes are dienes (unsaturated hydrocarbon alkene containing two carbon-to-carbon double bonds) with typical reactions of alkenes. Under basic conditions, they often convert to alkynes. In an allene, the two double bonds lie in planes that are perpendicular to each other. Consequently, in an allene of the type R1 R2 C=C=CR3 R4 , the groups R1 and R2 lie in a plane perpendicular to the plane containing R3 and R4 . Under these circumstances, the molecule is chiral (molecule whose arrangement of atoms is such that it cannot be superimposed on its mirror image) and can show optical activity.

A phenomenon in which parts and organs of the same organism grow at different rates. In other words, it is the growth in part of an organism in relation to its whole body. An example is legs increasing in length faster than the arms. It is studied by measuring the mass and size of any organ or part of the body and expressed in relation to the total mass or size of the entire organism using the relation Y = bx ⍺ , where Y is the mass of the organ, x is the mass of the organism, ⍺ is the coefficient of the organ and b is a constant. It is important in studying relative growth rates.

An allyl and derivatives formed by substitution. The term 'allylic position' or 'allylic site' refers to the saturated carbon atom. A group, such as -OH, attached at an allylic site is sometimes described as 'allylic'. An allyl group is a substituent with the structural formula H2 C=CH-CH2 R, where R is the connection to the rest of the molecule. Carbanions, carbenium ions or radicals, formally derived by detachment of one hydron, hydride or hydrogen from the CH3 group of propene or derivatives thereof. An example is allyl cation (H2 C=CHCH2 + ).

For example, if f ( x ) = 1 for all real x , g ( x ) = 1 for all irrational x and 0 for all rational x , then f and g agree almost everywhere, since the rationals have measure zero.
The powers of 2, because the aliquot parts (proper divisors) of 2 n sum to 2 n^-1. The only known almost perfect numbers are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ..., which form the powers of 2.

The disintegration of certain radioactive isotopes, causing the spontaneous emission of an alpha ( ) particle. An alpha particle is a stable particle formed from two protons and two neutrons and is identical to the nucleus of the helium atom. The general reaction for alpha decay is A Z X → A^-2 Z^-4 Y + 2 4 He , where X is the parent nuclide, Y is the daughter nuclide, Z is the atomic mass of X and A is the atomic number of X . The atomic number or the number of protons decreases by two and the mass number decreases by four as a result. Alpha decay commonly occurs in elements such as bismuth with atomic numbers greater than 83. It can occur in some rare-earth elements such as neodymium and lutetium with atomic numbers between 60 and 71.

A partial haemolysis (disintegration of red blood cells, with the release of haemoglobin) on blood agar plates (nutrient culture medium that is enriched with blood and used for the growth of certain strains of bacteria) as indicated by a green discolouration around the bacterial colony. It is caused by hydrogen peroxide produced by the bacterium, oxidising haemoglobin producing the green oxidised derivative, methemoglobin. Examples of α -haemolysis are Streptococcus pneumoniae that causes bacterial pneumonia and some other diseases; and Streptococcus viridans which causes dental infections some other diseases.

The most common form of secondary structure of proteins in which the polypeptide chain is coiled into a helix. This is a right-handed coiled or spiral conformation, in which every backbone N-H group donates a hydrogen bond to the backbone C=O group of the amino acid four residues earlier. The -helix is the most regular and the most predictable from sequence, as well as the most prevalent.

Electric current that changes direction periodically. If a graph of the current against time is plotted it is in a wave form, with its value varying periodically around zero. AC can come in a number of forms, as long as the voltage and current are alternating. The most common type of AC is the sine wave. The AC in homes and offices have an oscillating voltage that produces a sine wave. There are three parts to a sine wave: amplitude, frequency and phase. Some other waveforms include ths square waves, often used in digital and switching electronics to test their operation; and triangle waves, found in sound synthesis and are useful for testing linear electronics like amplifiers. The frequency of alternating current (AC) is measured in hertz. The frequency of the domestic supply is different in different parts of the world. In Europe and most parts of the world, it is 50 Hz and in the U.S., it is 60 Hz.

Clouds composed of flattened globules that may be arranged in groups. They are small, white, puffy clouds composed primarily of water droplets that sometimes slowly drift across the sky and forms at altitudes of between 2000 - 6000 metres above the ground with a vertical velocity of 0.05 ms^-1 to 0.1 m s^-1 . Altocumulus clouds usually form in a layer of moist air, where air currents undulate gently, like waves on the sea. As a wave rises, water vapour condenses and forms the cloud. For example, the function F ( x ) = x 5 /5 is an antiderivative of f ( x ) = x 4 . Since the derivative of a constant is zero, x 4 has an infinite number of antiderivatives such as ( x 5 /5) - 10, ( x 5 /5) + 2, etc. Thus, all the antiderivatives of x 4 can be obtained by changing the value of C in F ( x ) = ( x 5 /5) + C ; where C is an arbitrary constant known as the constant of integration. Basically, the graphs of antiderivatives of a given function are vertical translations of each other, with each graph's location depending on the value of C . Antiderivatives are related to definite integrals through the fundamental theorem of calculus and they are important because they can be used to compute definite integrals.

The reverse process of differentiation or a process of solving for antiderivatives. In other words, it is the process of finding an antiderivative for a given function; especially when deriving an indefinite integral or when evaluating a definite integral using the fundamental theorem of calculus rather than as an infinite sum of infinitesimal elements. A law of physics named after its discoverer, Archimedes of Syracuse that concerns the upward force or upthrust on any object fully or partly submerged in a fluid. It states that the buoyant force on an object is equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Mathematically, (buoyant force) Fb = m f g ... ., where m f is the mass of the fluid displaced by the body. Archimedes' principle can be expressed in other words that an object in a fluid such as water experiences an upthrust from the fluid which is equal to the weight of the fluid that the body displaces. The upward force is called the upthrust or buoyant force, expressed mathematically as: Upthrust = weight in air - weight in liquid. The resultant force on the A body is the difference between the upthrust and the body's weight. This difference is zero for a floating body, ie. upthrust and weight are equal and opposite. Hot air displaces a balloon, producing upthrust. This upthrust is balanced by the weight of the balloon. A hot air balloon rises when the upthrust on it is greater than its weight. A diver may attach lead weight to his suit if he wants to reach a greater depth. His weight will then be greater than the upthrust on him. For a given body to float in a given fluid depends on its weight and volume or the relative density (weight per unit volume). This is compared to that of the fluid in order to determine its buoyant force. If the body is less dense than the fluid, it will float. If the body is denser than the fluid, it will sink. The principle applies to both floating and submerged bodies and to all fluids, i.e., liquids and gases. Archimedes' principle is an important and underlying concept in the field of fluid mechanics.

The equilibrium constant K b for the base ionisation; or a reaction in which a weak base is in equilibrium with its conjugate acid in aqueous solution. For example, ammonia ionizes in water as follows: NH3( aq ) + H2 O ( l )  NH4 + ( aq ) + OH - ( aq ) The base-ionisation equilibrium constant is the mathematical product of the equilibrium concentrations of the products of this reaction divided by the equilibrium concentration of the original base. In other words, Kb is the product of the concentrations of the products over the concentration of the reactants (not including water). As the Kb value of a base increases, so does the strength of the base. For a strong base: K b > 1 and for a weak base: K b < 1. The value is sometimes expressed as the logarithm of its reciprocal, called pK b . Therefore pK b = -logK b . The smaller the value of pK b , the stronger the base. K b is a better measure of the strength of a base than pH because adding more water to the base solution will not change the value of the equilibrium constant K b , but it will change the H + ion concentration. Water is not included in the base-ionisation equilibrium expression because the [H2 O] has no effect on the equilibrium.

Any of 3000 species of bees divided into 19 families in the order Hymenoptera. The pollen they inevitably lose in going from flower to flower is important to plants because some pollen lands on the pistils of other flowers of the same species, resulting in cross-pollination. They are the most important pollinating insects and their interdependence with plants makes them good examples of the type of symbiosis called mutualism. Most bees have specialised branched or feathery body B hairs that help in the collection of pollen. Female bees, like many other hymenopterans, have a defensive sting. Some bees produce honey from flower nectar. Honey bees and stingless bees commonly store large quantities of honey, which is exploited by beekeepers, who harvest the honey for human consumption.

1. Sets in which experimental units are grouped in such a way that the units are similar as possible within each block. The experimental error associated with the block will be smaller than that obtained if the same number of units were randomly located within the whole experimental space. The blocks are generally determined by taking into account both controllable causes related by the factors studied and causes that may be difficult or impossible to keep constant over all of the experimentally units. The variations between the blocks are then eliminated when the effect of the factors are compared. Several types of regroupings can be used to reduce the effects of one or several sources of error. A randomized block design results if there is only one source of error. 2. In data management, a block is a group of records on a storage device. Blocks are manipulated as units. For example, disk drives often read and write data in 512-byte blocks. In word processing, a block is a contiguous set of characters, often consisting of a phrase, a sentence, a paragraph or a set of paragraphs that is selected by the user for copying/pasting, cutting or moving. But a block can consist of any contiguous set of characters, whether or not it forms a logical unit of text. In network communication, a block is a group of data bits or bytes that is transferred as a standard unit. The size or length of such a block depends on the communications protocol. A model of the atom conceived by Neil Bohr (1885-1962) in 1913 based on his observations of the atomic emissions spectrum of the hydrogen atom. The model assumes the following: (i) that the electrons revolve in orbits of specific radius around the nucleus without emitting or absorbing radiation; (ii) that within each orbit, an electron has a fixed amount of energy; and (iii) that emission or absorption of energy (photons) occurs between transitions. The energy absorbed or emitted can be calculated using the relation E2 - E1 = hf = h c λ , where E is the energy level, h is the Planck's constant (6.63 x 10 -34 Js, f is the frequency of the emitted photon, c is the speed of light (3.0 x 10 8 m/s) and λ is the wavelength.

A theory published in 1913 by Neils Bohr (1885-1962), a Danish physicist, which explains the line spectrum of hydrogen. It assumed that a single electron of mass m travelled in a circular orbit of radius r , at a velocity v , around a positively charged nucleus. The angular momentum of the electron would then be mvr . Bohr proposed that electrons could only occupy orbits in which this angular momentum had certain fixed values, h /2 π , 2 h /2 π , 3 h /2 π , ..., nh /2 π , where h is the Planck constant. This means that the angular momentum is quantized, i.e. it can only have certain values, each of which is a multiple of n . Each permitted value of n is associated with an orbit of different radius and Bohr assumed that when the atom emitted or absorbed radiation of frequency ν , the electron jumped from one orbit to another, with the energy emitted or absorbed by each jump being equal to hν . This theory gave good results in predicting the lines observed in the spectrum of hydrogen and simple ions such as He + , Li 2+ , etc. The idea of quantized values of angular momentum was later explained by the wave nature of the electron. Each orbit has a whole number of wavelengths around it; i.e. nλ = 2 πr , where λ is the wavelength and n a whole number. The wavelength of a particle is given by h / mv , so nh / mv = 2 πr , which leads to mvr = nh /2 π . Modern atomic theory does not allow subatomic particles to be treated in the same way as large objects and Bohr's reasoning is somewhat discredited. However, the idea of quantized angular momentum has been retained.

A strong force of attraction holding atoms together in a molecule or crystal. In other words, it is the electrostatic force of attraction between two chemical species (ions, atoms, molecules). The various types include the following: (i) ionic or electrovalent bond that is created during the formation of a compound by transfer of one or more electrons from one atom to another, the resulting oppositely charged ions being held together by attraction; (ii) covalent bond , in which the attractive force between atoms is created by the sharing of electrons; and (iii) metallic bond , which is the electrostatic force between delocalised electrons and positively charged metal ions characteristic of metals. The electrons are shared between atoms and move about in the crystal. Typically chemical bonds have energies of about 1000 kJ mol^-1 .

A nuclear reactor that produces more fissionable materials than it uses. The reactor is built with a core of fissionable plutonium, Pu^-239 and surrounded by a layer of U^-238. As the Pu^-239 undergoes spontaneous fission, it releases neutrons which convert U^-238 to Pu^-239. After all the U^-238 has been changed to Pu^-239, the reactor is refuelled. Some disadvantages of this breeder reactor are: (i) Pu^-239 is very toxic; (ii) the half-life of U^-239 is extremely long, about 24,000 years; this could create an almost impossible disposal problem if large amounts of this material are generated; (iii) because of the nature of the reactor core, water cannot be used as a coolant, so liquid sodium must be used. In the event of an accident a catastrophe could develop because sodium reacts violently with water and air.
